timeline.event: Mexican Revolution convulses the country; Washington watches and intervenes as factions fight for power.
U.S. Navy occupies Veracruz after the Tampico Affair, one of the sharpest pre–World War I clashes.
Pershing’s punitive expedition chases Pancho Villa deep into northern Mexico, straining sovereignty.
Mexico enters World War II on the Allied side; wartime partnership rebuilds trust after decades of friction.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Mexican oil expropriation (wartime context)

timeline.event: President Truman returns captured Mexican battle flags from the 1846–48 war, a symbolic reconciliation.
Bracero Program (1942–1964) brings millions of Mexican guest workers north, tying labor markets together.
Chamizal Treaty settles a century-old El Paso–Juárez border dispute; land is swapped peacefully.
Boundary Treaty of 1970 resolves remaining Rio Grande channel shifts and sets rules for future changes.
Mexico’s debt crisis and peso collapse roil the economy; the U.S. helps stabilize its major trading partner.
NAFTA enters into force, locking Canada, Mexico, and the U.S. into a shared North American market.
Clinton arranges a $20 billion rescue package after the peso crisis, repaid ahead of schedule in 1997.
Mexico condemns the 9/11 attacks and aids U.S. hurricane relief, but stays out of the Iraq War.
Mérida Initiative launches deep U.S.–Mexico security cooperation against drug cartels and arms trafficking.
Border-wall rhetoric and tariff threats under Trump; Pew finds Mexican confidence in the U.S. plunges.

NYT: Peña Nieto cancels Trump meeting

timeline.event: Washington and Mexico City agree on an updated NAFTA framework alongside Canada (later USMCA).

notes_summary: From Tsarist recognition and the Alaska sale through a WWII alliance, a long Cold War, a 1990s reset, and a post-2014 rupture—now defined by Ukraine, sanctions, and broken arms-control treaties.

timeline.event: The Russian Empire recognizes the United States (1803) and the two capitals exchange diplomats in 1809, opening a channel that lasts until 1917.

links.label: Oxford Research Encyclopedia: U.S.–Russian relations before 1917

timeline.event: The Russo-American Treaty sets 54°40′ N as the southern edge of Russian America, cooling a Pacific boundary fight after the Ukase of 1821.

links.label: Oxford Research Encyclopedia: U.S.–Russian relations before 1917

timeline.event: Russian fleets winter in New York and San Francisco during the Civil War; Union crowds treat the visit as friendly solidarity against Britain and France.

links.label: U.S. Naval History: The Russian Navy Visits the United States

timeline.event: Alaska Purchase: Russia sells the colony to the United States for $7.2 million, exiting North America and expanding U.S. Pacific reach.
Theodore Roosevelt mediates the Treaty of Portsmouth ending the Russo-Japanese War and later wins the Nobel Peace Prize for the talks.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Treaty of Portsmouth

timeline.event: Washington abrogates the 1832 commercial treaty to protest pogroms and discrimination against Jews, including U.S. citizens traveling in the Empire.
After the February Revolution, the United States is first to recognize Russia’s Provisional Government and extends large wartime credits.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Recognition of the Soviet Union

timeline.event: U.S. troops join Allied interventions in North Russia and Siberia; the failed campaigns and Bolshevik victory lock in years of non-recognition.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Recognition of the Soviet Union

timeline.event: The Roosevelt–Litvinov agreements finally recognize the USSR—the last major power to do so—while debt and Comintern disputes are deferred.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Recognition of the Soviet Union, 1933
NYT Learning Network: U.S. establishes relations with the USSR

timeline.event: After Barbarossa and Pearl Harbor, Lend-Lease trucks, food, and aircraft make the United States and USSR wartime allies against Nazi Germany.
Yalta shapes postwar Europe while U.S. and Soviet troops meet at the Elbe; within months, arguments over Poland and Germany replace the wartime glow.
The Truman Doctrine and Marshall Plan lock in containment; Moscow rejects the aid terms for its sphere and the Cold War becomes policy.
The Berlin Blockade and Airlift freeze Germany’s split; NATO is founded in 1949 as the Soviet atomic test ends the U.S. nuclear monopoly.

links.label: Office of the Historian: North Atlantic Treaty Organization, 1949

timeline.event: The Berlin Crisis and the Wall seal the city’s divide; Checkpoint Charlie’s tank standoff becomes an emblem of superpower nerve.
The Cuban Missile Crisis brings the superpowers to the nuclear brink before a quarantine, secret bargaining, and Soviet withdrawal defuse it.
Nixon’s Moscow Summit produces SALT I and the ABM Treaty—détente’s core arms-control architecture after years of crisis.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Helsinki Final Act / détente

timeline.event: The Helsinki Final Act recognizes postwar borders while inserting human-rights baskets that dissidents later turn against Moscow.

links.label: Office of the Historian: Helsinki Final Act, 1975

timeline.event: After the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan, Carter shelves SALT II, embargoes grain, and arms the mujahideen—détente collapses.
Reagan and Gorbachev sign the INF Treaty in Washington, eliminating a whole class of ground-launched missiles with on-site verification.

links.label: RFE/RL: INF and START nuclear context

timeline.event: The USSR dissolves; Russia takes the U.N. Security Council seat and nuclear command as Bush and Yeltsin proclaim partnership and Nunn–Lugar work begins.

links.label: National Security Archive: Bush–Yeltsin telephone memo, Dec. 1991
